@graph.headline: 60.5% of Y Combinator companies can be email-spoofed
@graph.description: A scan of all 6,157 Y Combinator company domains found 60.5% publish no DMARC record or a policy of p=none, leaving them open to email spoofing. First run August 14, 2026; re-run in full September 3, 2026.

@graph.name: YC company DMARC posture, August and September 2026
@graph.description: DMARC policy, SPF presence and MX status for 6,157 unique Y Combinator company domains, with batch and industry labels. Two full runs, August 14 and September 3, 2026, plus the list of every domain whose verdict changed between them.
@graph.measurementTechnique: Passive public DNS resolution of _dmarc TXT, SPF TXT and MX records

acceptedAnswer.text: A domain is spoofable if it publishes no DMARC record, or a DMARC policy of p=none. Both cases mean a forged message showing the domain's exact From address will still be delivered. Protection begins at p=quarantine and is complete at p=reject.

mainEntity.name: Does having SPF stop email spoofing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. SPF validates the hidden envelope sender, not the From header a recipient sees. In this study 73.1% of spoofable domains published a valid SPF record. Without a DMARC policy at enforcement, SPF alone does not stop From-header spoofing.

mainEntity.name: How do I check whether my own domain can be spoofed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Enter your domain at notspoofed.com for a free check of your SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, or run dig +short TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com and look at the p= value.

mainEntity.name: How quickly are companies moving to DMARC enforcement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Slowly. Between a scan on August 14, 2026 and a full re-scan on September 3, 2026, 56 of 5,959 Y Combinator company domains moved to p=quarantine or p=reject and 16 moved the other way, so the spoofable share of that stable cohort fell from 60.9% to 60.2%. Companies newly added to the directory in the same period were 75.6% spoofable.
